title: Leaf Area, Canopy Photosynthesis, and Self-Shading
objective: Scale from a single leaf to a layered canopy and use leaf area, light distribution, leaf age, and spatial uniformity to evaluate productive canopy structure.

terms.definition: One-sided leaf area per unit ground or bench area.
Progressive reduction of photon flux through a canopy by absorption, reflection, and transmission.
Integrated carbon exchange of all leaves and non-leaf tissues in the canopy.
Shading of a plant's leaves or reproductive tissues by its own architecture.

coreScience: Canopy carbon gain depends on intercepted photons and how efficiently leaves at different depths use them. Upper leaves receive more direct light and can saturate or overheat while lower leaves remain below useful rates. Leaf angle, size, spacing, internode length, branch distribution, plant density, spectrum, and fixture geometry shape the light profile.

Adding leaf area initially increases interception, but gains diminish as overlap increases. Very dense canopies create persistent shade, high humidity, weak airflow, and low-productivity leaves. Excessive removal has the opposite cost: less photon interception, fewer reserves, and reduced capacity to support roots and flowers.

A cannabis density experiment found that plant density and architecture changed yield per plant, yield per area, lower-canopy leaf drying and light deprivation, and cannabinoid uniformity under the tested system. Those outcomes are system-specific. A high top-canopy PPFD reading cannot establish uniform exposure, and more grams per plant can coincide with fewer grams per area.
cultivationRelevance: Map light on a grid at the actual canopy plane and repeat after major training or stretch. Include lower-canopy measurements when vertical uniformity matters.

Use pruning and spacing to create a functional canopy, not a naked stem. Preserve enough healthy leaf area for interception while removing clearly unproductive, diseased, or airflow-blocking material under a defined plan.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Area, height, depth, plant density, branch distribution, and leaf-area method.
Grid coordinates, PPFD, DLI, sensor, height, fixture settings, and uniformity metric.
Temperature, RH/VPD, airflow, CO2, and leaf temperature by depth.
Spacing, topping, bending, trellis, pruning, defoliation, and date/stage.
Biomass per plant/area, flower position, chemistry sampling position, and disease incidence.

misconceptions: Every shaded leaf is useless: Lower leaves may contribute positive carbon and stored nutrients depending on their light and age.
Maximum leaf area is always best: Beyond useful interception, density can increase respiration, shade, humidity, and disease risk.
Top-canopy PPFD describes the crop: A map and canopy-depth profile are required.
evidenceLimits: Leaf-area index and canopy photosynthesis are method-dependent. Destructive leaf-area measurements, image segmentation, and light-extinction models each carry sampling and geometry errors.
